newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb lawyers seeking more information. [CORRECTED 23:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb lawyers seeking more information. [CORRECTED 23:40 GMT]

text.p: Attorneys in the Oklahoma City bombing trial will be back in court Wednesday for a pre-trial hearing on how much more information about the case prosecutors must turn over to the defence.
Prosecutors have already turned over more than 160,000 pages of material and argue they have gone beyond the rules to provide defence lawyers with information they have requested.

Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols have been charged in the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed the lives of 168 people. They are expected to be present at the hearing.
The two will be tried separately sometime next year. U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch may announce the date of the first trial, James Manspeaker, the clerk of the federal court, said.
(Corrects to drop reference to possible announcement of first trial being made Wednesday)
McVeigh's lawyers have raised the possibility the bombing may have been the work of international terrorists or that the government may have had some advance knowledge of the bombing.

The defence team said it wanted information prosecutors may have about bomb threats in Oklahoma City and claimed that no Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms agents were in the building at the time of the bombing.

Prosecutors said neither the ATF nor any other federal agency had prior knowledge of the bombing and called the suggestion "specious." They also said five ATF agents were in the Murrah building at the time of the bombing.

Prosecutors also reject suggestions that the Oklahoma sheriff's bomb squad training was connected to the bombing or that the Israeli or Kuwaiti governments warned the U.S. government of possible terrorist attacks against the building.

The judge will also hear arguments on establishing criteria for who will be admitted to the closed circuit televised proceedings in Oklahoma City. The closed broadcast will be for the benefit of victims who will not be able to attend the trials in Denver, which have been moved here due to publicity over the bombing in Oklahoma.
